issues.legal_issue: Members whose admission preceded the admission of other members retain seniority when their membership was later regularised after defects in their affidavits were corrected.
material_facts: Fifteen members had been admitted before the appellants were admitted. Their membership was kept in abeyance because their affidavits lacked full information, and the Society regularised their membership after they supplied corrected affidavits.
The appellants’ membership was first approved after the fifteen members had already been admitted; the fifteen members’ membership was regularised at that later meeting.
issues.conclusion: The fifteen members ranked senior to the appellants for the allotment process because their membership had been admitted earlier; the High Court’s conclusion disclosed no error warranting interference.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court found no basis to interfere with the High Court’s factual conclusion that the earlier-admitted members were senior. Later regularisation of membership did not alter the fact that those members had been admitted before the appellants.

rule.if: plot_allotment_seniority_dispute and earlier_members_admitted_first and earlier_membership_only_held_in_abeyance_for_affidavit_defects and corrected_affidavits_submitted and later_members_admitted_afterward

predicates.plot_allotment_seniority_dispute: The proceeding disputes the seniority of members used to determine priority in a plot-allotment process.
predicates.earlier_members_admitted_first: The members whose seniority is disputed were admitted before the other members.
predicates.earlier_membership_only_held_in_abeyance: The earlier members’ membership was held in abeyance because their affidavits lacked required information.
predicates.corrected_affidavits_submitted: The earlier members supplied corrected affidavits, after which their membership was regularised.
predicates.later_members_admitted_afterward: The other members were admitted after the earlier members had been admitted.

issues.definition: When a plot-allotment seniority dispute concerns members admitted earlier whose membership was only held in abeyance for affidavit defects later corrected, they rank ahead of members admitted afterward.

issues.legal_issue: An authority empowered to exempt a cooperative society from an otherwise applicable requirement may permit an amended bye-law to operate retrospectively where that effect is within the exemption power, serves the amendment’s purpose, and is not unreasonable or made in bad faith.
material_facts: A cooperative society amended its membership bye-law to include employees of departments that had been part of a particular ministry, and the Registrar registered the amendment after the Lieutenant Governor allowed the Society’s appeal against refusal to register it.

The Lieutenant Governor’s appellate decision was intended to regularise the membership of persons who had joined the Society years earlier and whose names had figured in the membership information used in connection with the Society’s land allotment.
A later notification exempted the Society from the statutory rule governing when registered bye-law amendments came into operation and specified an earlier effective date for the amended bye-law.

The retrospective date corresponded to the date on which the first member in the affected category had applied for enrolment. The appellants challenged the notification and the resulting eligibility and approval of members.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective-effect notification was within the Lieutenant Governor’s exemption power and was valid. The legal fiction created by the notification meant that approvals of affected members made before the bye-law was formally registered were not invalid merely because they preceded registration.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 88 of the Delhi Cooperative Societies Act, 1972, respectively addressed when a registered amendment ordinarily came into force and empowered the Lieutenant Governor to exempt a society from provisions of the Act or apply them with modifications. The Court read the notification in substance, including supplying an apparently omitted word in light of its context and Hindi version, relying on Surjit Singh v. Kalra, Hameedia Hardware Stores v. B. Mohan Lal Sowcar, and Sirajul Haq Khan v. Sunni Central Board of Waqf. It held that the notification was not unreasonable or mala fide, applying Kruse v. Johnson and considering Partap Singh v. State of Punjab. The exemption also served, rather than defeated, the Act’s policy, consistently with Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Trivandrum v. K. Kunhambu. Under the principle in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council, the consequences of the deemed earlier effective date followed; B. Shama Rao v. Union Territory of Pondicherry was distinguishable.

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_cooperative_b: The proceeding challenges retrospective operation of a cooperative society’s amended membership bye-law under an exemption granted by an authority.
predicates.law_authorized_exemption_from_effective_: The governing law authorized the authority to exempt a society from the otherwise applicable requirement governing when a registered bye-law amendment takes effect.
predicates.retrospective_effect_served_the_amendmen: The earlier effective date enabled the amendment to regularise the membership of people who had joined the society before the amendment was registered.
predicates.manifestly_unreasonable_or_made_in_bad_f: The exemption was manifestly unreasonable or was made in bad faith.

issues.definition: Where a challenge concerns retrospective operation of an amended cooperative bye-law, the law authorizes an exemption from the ordinary effective-date requirement, and the earlier date serves the amendment’s purpose without manifest unreasonableness or bad faith, the retrospective operation is valid.

issues.legal_issue: An authority cannot rescind an instrument in a way that effectively reviews and nullifies its final quasi-judicial decision when no power of review has been conferred.
material_facts: The Lieutenant Governor had allowed the Society’s appeal against the Registrar’s refusal to register a membership amendment and had issued a final quasi-judicial decision directing the amendment.
A later notification purported to rescind the earlier notification that had given the amendment retrospective effect, without expressly rescinding the earlier quasi-judicial decision.

In practical effect, the later notification nullified that decision. The earlier decision and notification had also created substantive rights for affected members, and the Act conferred no power to review the quasi-judicial decision.
issues.conclusion: The later rescission notification was ultra vires and invalid because it effectively nullified a final quasi-judicial decision without a conferred power of review; it was also invalid insofar as it took away rights created by the earlier decision and notification.
issues.legal_principle: A final quasi-judicial order cannot be reviewed by the authority that made it unless a power of review has specifically been conferred. The order was made under Section 76 of the Delhi Cooperative Societies Act, 1972, which conferred no such review power. The Court relied on G.V. Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh for the rule that general powers to exercise a function from time to time do not authorise review of a quasi-judicial order, and on State of Kerala v. K.G. Madhavan Pillai for the principle that a general power to rescind cannot be used to take away rights already acquired under an earlier order. The rescission power was considered in relation to Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

rule.if: challenge_to_rescission_of_final_quasijudicial_decision and ((earlier_decision_was_final and later_action_effectively_nullified_it and no_review_power_was_conferred) or (earlier_action_created_enforceable_rights and later_action_took_them_away))

predicates.challenge_to_rescission_of_final_quasiju: The proceeding challenges a later rescission that affects an earlier quasi-judicial decision.
predicates.earlier_decision_was_final: The earlier quasi-judicial decision had become final.
predicates.later_action_effectively_nullified_it: The later action effectively nullified the earlier decision, even though it did not expressly rescind that decision.
predicates.no_review_power_was_conferred: The governing law did not confer power on the decision-maker to review the earlier decision.
predicates.earlier_action_created_enforceable_right: The earlier decision and related action created rights enforceable by the affected persons.
predicates.later_action_took_them_away: The later action took away rights created by the earlier decision and related action.

issues.definition: A rescission challenged in a proceeding of this kind is invalid if it effectively nullifies a final quasi-judicial decision without review authority or takes away enforceable rights created by the earlier action.
